claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself; a migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Pulumi component state migrations are a new feature.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering component state migrations and the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repo contains the aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration example with three programs (v1, v2, v3) and migration code.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ about components.
In the example's v1, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the example, a security group sits outside the VPC component and refers to the VPC.
Because an AWS security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC would mean replacing the security group too (per AWS CloudFormation docs on the EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId property).
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, an upgrade from legacy AWSX VPC to modern could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
The example does not create a database.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data.
The example's v2 upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The example's v3 removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example's resource trees, v1 tracks awsx:x:ec2:Vpc with children aws Vpc, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet (with subnet, route table, association), and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway (with internet gateway); v2 tracks awsx:ec2:Vpc with aws Vpc, subnet vpc-isolated-1, route table, association, and internet gateway under it; v3 has plain aws resources only.
In Pulumi state, each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
Aliases cannot remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources; a state migration is needed for that.
To migrate to modern AWSX, the new VPC component is registered with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option.
The example's `migrateClassicVpc` is defined in aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
The alias lets Pulumi find the old component; the migration callback receives the component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A state migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records replacing the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
In the example's migration callback, if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record, changes its URN, type, and parent, and preserves the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.
Entries in `successors` let the Pulumi engine know old and new records map to the same new record, and Pulumi uses them to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
In the example, the two subnet entries in `successors` map the old component wrapper and the managed subnet to the same new subnet record.
The example's v3 declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.

The example's second migration removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, and the VPC keeps its AWS ID.
The second migration is at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
In the example, the plain VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already on modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means users can skip versions without editing stack state by hand.
After a migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In the example, upgrades can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags even though resource IDs are kept.
To try the example, start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
Before each upgrade in the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component registers its migration in its implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls.
Pulumi resource state migration callbacks run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
Pulumi resource state migration callbacks must be idempotent.
Pulumi resource state migration callbacks must return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi resource state migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi state migrations option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the callback API.

Component state migration state entries use the checkpoint resource format documented in the Pulumi developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state), including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
A Pulumi component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of Pulumi component state migrations (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
